doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Ghosted rock bands and the Wrecking Crew
summary: After Rowe's Manny Albam story, he says studio players ghosted on rock records like the Byrds', Glen Campbell included.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Yeah. I had a funny, Manny Albam had a funny anecdote about, I think he was producing the Guess Who.

Manny Albam. Anyway, the band struggled for like two or three days to get the rhythm track down and then he calls in all these pros, guys like Bill Watrous. And the band is going, “How did they do that?” And he goes, “Well they play music.”

Yeah well the thing is there’s a lot of records of rock bands of the day — the Beatles played their own stuff of course, but there were some well known bands that were ghosted as they say. It was the Wrecking Crew in LA on a lot of pop and rock records that were supposed to be the band playing. I won’t tell you who, but you can find out. But © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

it was the same thing. Do you want to spend three days trying to cut a mediocre track or 20 minutes to cut an exceptional track. Guess what wins. But there were millions of dollars spent, tens of millions spent on bands trying to cut their own tracks. I mean there were some certainly that could, but even like things like the Byrds. I mean they played but hey guess who also was in there playing 12-string? Glen Campbell as a session player. But that just comes with the territory. You don’t think okay they’re out there millions of dollars, I’m in here making double scale. And they’re getting royalties, I’m not getting royalties. But that was your job.
